turns.replyText:
Can you explain the main options in simple terms?

Absolutely, I can break this down simply.

When you’re choosing roses with us, you’re mainly deciding between a few big things:

Where you live (hardiness zone)
Every rose has a “zone range” (like zones 5–9) where it will be happy.
On our site you can pick your zone at the top; then you’ll only see roses that should do well where you live.
How big you want the plant to be
Bush / shrub roses: These are rounded plants that stay in one spot and make lots of blooms. Good for beds and borders.
Climbing roses: These make long canes you tie to an arch, trellis, or fence. Great if you want a “wall” of flowers but they do need support.
Groundcover / landscape roses: These stay low and spread out, good for covering a slope or the front of a border.
Flower style
Hybrid tea type: Classic “long-stemmed” rose look, usually one big flower per stem. Nice for cutting and vases.
Floribunda / cluster type: Many medium-sized blooms in clusters, so the whole shrub looks very full of flowers.
Old-fashioned / English style: Very full, many-petaled blooms that look like peonies. Often strongly fragrant.
How often they bloom
Repeat or continuous bloomers: Flower, rest, flower again through the season. Most people new to roses like these because you get color for a long time.
Once-bloomers: One big, spectacular show, usually in late spring or early summer, then mostly just foliage. Lovely but less constant color.
Fragrance and color
Fragrance can be light, medium, or strong. If scent matters to you, you can filter for fragrance level.
Color is just personal taste; you can filter by pink, red, yellow, white, apricot, etc.

A couple of basics about our roses

We sell only own-root roses in 1-gallon containers with soil (not bare root).
They are defoliated (no leaves or buds) when they arrive, then leaf out after planting.
They must be grown outdoors in full sun (about 6 or more hours of direct sun a day is best).

They’re surprised it’s not as hard as they expected
Beginners often say they were nervous at first, but once they followed the planting guide, the roses settled in and started growing well. Many say things like “I’m new to roses and this one is thriving” or “I thought roses were fussy, but this was easier than I expected.”

They appreciate that own-root roses are forgiving
New gardeners like knowing that:

There’s no graft/bud union to worry about.
If something goes wrong, the plant can regrow from its own roots as the same variety. They often mention feeling more confident because they don’t have to figure out which canes are “rootstock” vs. the real rose.

They love the payoff once blooms start
